{{Short description|Vector bundle existing over a Grassmannian}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''tautological bundle''' is a [[vector bundle]] occurring over a [[Grassmannian]] in a natural tautological way: for a Grassmannian of <math>k</math>-[[dimension (vector space)|dimensional]] [[linear subspace|subspaces]] of <math>V</math>, given a point in the Grassmannian corresponding to a <math>k</math>-dimensional vector subspace <math>W \subseteq V</math>, the fiber over <math>W</math> is the subspace <math>W</math> itself. In the case of [[projective space]] the tautological bundle is known as the '''tautological line bundle.'''

The tautological bundle is also called the '''[[universal bundle]]''' since any vector bundle (over a compact space<ref>Over a noncompact but paracompact base, this remains true provided one uses infinite Grassmannian.</ref>) is a pullback of the tautological bundle; this is to say a Grassmannian is a [[classifying space]] for vector bundles. Because of this, the tautological bundle is important in the study of [[characteristic class]]es.

Tautological bundles are constructed both in [[algebraic topology]] and in algebraic geometry. In algebraic geometry, the tautological line bundle (as [[invertible sheaf]]) is

:<math>\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^n}(-1),</math>

the [[dual bundle|dual]] of the '''hyperplane bundle''' or [[Serre's twisting sheaf]] <math>\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^n}(1)</math>. The hyperplane bundle is the line bundle corresponding to the hyperplane ([[divisor (algebraic geometry)|divisor]]) <math>\mathbb{P}^{n-1}</math> in <math>\mathbb{P}^n</math>. The tautological line bundle and the hyperplane bundle are exactly the two generators of the [[Picard group]] of the projective space.<ref>In literature and textbooks, both are often called canonical generators.</ref>

In [[Michael Atiyah]]'s "K-theory", the tautological line bundle over a [[complex projective space]] is called the '''standard line bundle'''. The sphere bundle of the standard bundle is usually called the [[Hopf bundle]]. (cf. [[Bott generator]].)

More generally, there are also tautological bundles on a [[projective bundle]] of a vector bundle, as well as a [[Grassmann bundle]].

The older term ''canonical bundle'' has dropped out of favour, on the grounds that ''[[canonical (disambiguation)|canonical]]'' is already a heavily overloaded term, in both mathematical terminology and confusion with the [[canonical class]] in [[algebraic geometry]] could scarcely be avoided.

== Intuitive definition ==

Grassmannians by definition are the parameter spaces for [[linear subspace]]s, of a given dimension, in a given [[vector space]] <math>W</math>. If <math>G</math> is a Grassmannian, and <math>V_g</math> is the subspace of <math>W</math> corresponding to <math>g</math> in <math>G</math>, this is already almost the data required for a vector bundle: namely a vector space for each point <math>g</math>, varying continuously. All that can stop the definition of the tautological bundle from this indication, is the difficulty that the <math>V_g</math> are going to intersect. Fixing this up is a routine application of the [[disjoint union]] device, so that the bundle projection is from a [[Fiber bundle|total space]] made up of identical copies of the <math>V_g</math>, that now do not intersect. With this, we have the bundle.

The projective space case is included. By convention <math>P(V)</math> may usefully carry the tautological bundle in the [[dual space]] sense. That is, with <math>V^*</math> the dual space, points of <math>P(V)</math> carry the vector subspaces of <math>V^*</math> that are their kernels, when considered as (rays of) [[linear functional]]s on <math>V^*</math>. If <math>V</math> has dimension <math>n+1</math>, the tautological [[line bundle]] is one tautological bundle, and the other, just described, is of rank <math>n</math>.

== Formal definition ==
Let <math>G_n(\R^{n+k})</math> be the [[Grassmannian]] of ''n''-dimensional vector subspaces in <math>\R^{n+k};</math> as a set it is the set of all ''n''-dimensional vector subspaces of <math>\R^{n+k}.</math> For example, if ''n'' = 1, it is the real projective ''k''-space.

We define the tautological bundle γ<sub>''n'', ''k''</sub> over <math>G_n(\R^{n+k})</math> as follows. The total space of the bundle is the set of all pairs (''V'', ''v'') consisting of a point ''V'' of the Grassmannian and a vector ''v'' in ''V''; it is given the [[subspace topology]] of the Cartesian product <math>G_n(\R^{n+k}) \times \R^{n+k}.</math> The projection map π is given by π(''V'', ''v'') = ''V''. If ''F'' is the pre-image of ''V'' under π, it is given a structure of a vector space by ''a''(''V'', ''v'') + ''b''(''V'', ''w'') = (''V'', ''av'' + ''bw''). Finally, to see local triviality, given a point ''X'' in the Grassmannian, let ''U'' be the set of all ''V'' such that the orthogonal projection ''p'' onto ''X'' maps ''V'' isomorphically onto ''X'',<ref>''U'' is open since <math>G_n(\R^{n+k})</math> is given a topology such that

:<math>\begin{cases} G_n(\R^{n+k}) \to \operatorname{End}(\R^{n+k}) \\ V \mapsto p_V \end{cases}</math>

where <math>p_V</math> is the orthogonal projection onto ''V'', is a homeomorphism onto the image.</ref> and then define

:<math>\begin{cases} \phi: \pi^{-1}(U) \to U\times X\subseteq  G_n(\R^{n+k}) \times X \\ \phi(V,v) = (V, p(v)) \end{cases}</math>

which is clearly a [[homeomorphism]]. Hence, the result is a vector bundle of rank ''n''.

The above definition continues to make sense if we replace <math>\R</math> with the [[complex field]] <math>\C.</math>

By definition, the infinite Grassmannian <math>G_n</math> is the [[direct limit]] of <math>G_n(\R^{n+k})</math> as <math>k\to\infty.</math> Taking the direct limit of the bundles γ<sub>''n'', ''k''</sub> gives the tautological bundle γ<sub>''n''</sub> of <math>G_n.</math> It is a universal bundle in the sense: for each compact space ''X'', there is a natural bijection

:<math>\begin{cases} [X, G_n] \to \operatorname{Vect}^{\R}_n(X) \\ f \mapsto f^*(\gamma_n) \end{cases}</math>

where on the left the bracket means homotopy class and on the right is the set of isomorphism classes of real vector bundles of rank ''n''. The inverse map is given as follows: since ''X'' is compact, any vector bundle ''E'' is a [[subbundle]] of a trivial bundle: <math>E \hookrightarrow X \times \R^{n+k}</math> for some ''k'' and so ''E'' determines a map 

:<math>\begin{cases}f_E: X \to G_n \\ x \mapsto E_x \end{cases}</math>

unique up to homotopy.

'''Remark''': In turn, one can define a tautological bundle as a universal bundle; suppose there is a natural bijection

:<math>[X, G_n] = \operatorname{Vect}^{\R}_n(X)</math>

for any [[paracompact space]] ''X''. Since <math>G_n</math> is the direct limit of compact spaces, it is paracompact and so there is a unique vector bundle over <math>G_n</math> that corresponds to the identity map on <math>G_n.</math> It is precisely the tautological bundle and, by restriction, one gets the tautological bundles over all <math>G_n(\R^{n+k}).</math>

== Hyperplane bundle ==
The '''hyperplane bundle''' ''H'' on a real projective ''k''-space is defined as follows. The total space of ''H'' is the set of all pairs (''L'', ''f'') consisting of a line ''L'' through the origin in <math>\R^{k+1}</math> and ''f'' a linear functional on ''L''. The projection map π is given by π(''L'', ''f'') = ''L'' (so that the fiber over ''L'' is the dual vector space of ''L''.) The rest is exactly like the tautological line bundle.

In other words, ''H'' is the [[dual bundle]] of the tautological line bundle.

In algebraic geometry, the hyperplane bundle is the line bundle (as [[invertible sheaf]]) corresponding to the '''hyperplane divisor'''

:<math>H = \mathbb{P}^{n-1} \sub \mathbb{P}^{n}</math>

given as, say, ''x''<sub>0</sub> = 0, when ''x<sub>i</sub>'' are the [[homogeneous coordinate]]s. This can be seen as follows. If ''D'' is a [[Weil divisor|(Weil) divisor]] on <math>X=\mathbb{P}^n,</math> one defines the corresponding line bundle ''O''(''D'') on ''X'' by 

:<math>\Gamma(U, O(D)) = \{ f \in K | (f) + D \ge 0 \text{ on } U \}</math>

where ''K'' is the field of rational functions on ''X''. Taking ''D'' to be ''H'', we have:

:<math>\begin{cases}O(H) \simeq O(1)\\ f \mapsto f x_0\end{cases}</math>

where ''x''<sub>0</sub> is, as usual, viewed as a global section of the twisting sheaf ''O''(1). (In fact, the above isomorphism is part of the usual correspondence between Weil divisors and Cartier divisors.) Finally, the dual of the twisting sheaf corresponds to the tautological line bundle (see below).

==Tautological line bundle in algebraic geometry==

In algebraic geometry, this notion exists over any field ''k''. The concrete definition is as follows. Let <math>A = k[y_0, \dots, y_n]</math> and <math>\mathbb{P}^n = \operatorname{Proj}A</math>. Note that we have:

:<math>\mathbf{Spec} \left (\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^n}[x_0, \ldots, x_n] \right ) = \mathbb{A}^{n+1}_{\mathbb{P}^n} = \mathbb{A}^{n+1} \times_k {\mathbb{P}^n}</math>

where '''Spec''' is [[relative Spec]]. Now, put:

:<math>L = \mathbf{Spec} \left (\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^n}[x_0, \dots, x_n]/I \right )</math>

where ''I'' is the [[ideal sheaf]] generated by global sections <math>x_iy_j-x_jy_i</math>. Then ''L'' is a closed subscheme of <math>\mathbb{A}^{n+1}_{\mathbb{P}^n}</math> over the same base scheme <math>\mathbb{P}^n</math>; moreover, the closed points of ''L'' are exactly those (''x'', ''y'') of <math>\mathbb{A}^{n+1} \times_k \mathbb{P}^n</math> such that either ''x'' is zero or the image of ''x'' in <math>\mathbb{P}^n</math> is ''y''. Thus, ''L'' is the tautological line bundle as defined before if ''k'' is the field of real or complex numbers.

In more concise terms, ''L'' is the [[blowing up|blow-up]] of the origin of the affine space <math>\mathbb{A}^{n+1}</math>, where the locus ''x'' = 0 in ''L'' is the [[exceptional divisor]]. (cf. Hartshorne, Ch. I, the end of § 4.)

In general, <math>\mathbf{Spec}(\operatorname{Sym} \check{E})</math> is the [[algebraic vector bundle]] corresponding to a locally free sheaf ''E'' of finite rank.<ref>Editorial note: this definition differs from Hartshorne in that he does not take dual, but is consistent with the standard practice and the other parts of Wikipedia.</ref> Since we have the [[exact sequence]]:

:<math>0 \to I \to \mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^n}[x_0, \ldots, x_n] \overset{x_i \mapsto y_i}{\longrightarrow} \operatorname{Sym} \mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^n}(1) \to 0,</math>

the tautological line bundle ''L'', as defined above, corresponds to the dual <math>\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^n}(-1)</math> of [[Serre's twisting sheaf]]. In practice both the notions (tautological line bundle and the dual of the twisting sheaf) are used interchangeably.

Over a field, its dual line bundle is the line bundle associated to the [[hyperplane divisor]] ''H'', whose global sections are the [[linear forms]]. Its [[Chern class]] is −''H''. This is an example of  an anti-[[ample line bundle]]. Over <math>\C,</math> this is equivalent to saying that it is a negative line bundle, meaning that  minus its Chern class is the [[de Rham cohomology|de Rham class]] of the standard [[Kähler form]].

==Facts==

*The tautological line bundle γ<sub>1, ''k''</sub> is  [[fiber bundle|locally trivial]] but not [[fiber bundle#Examples|trivial]], for ''k'' ≥ 1. This remains true over other fields.{{citation needed|date=December 2014}}

In fact, it is straightforward to show that, for ''k'' = 1, the real tautological line bundle is none other than the well-known bundle whose [[fiber bundle|total space]] is the [[Möbius strip]]. For a full proof of the above fact, see.<ref>{{harvnb|Milnor|Stasheff|1974|loc=§2. Theorem 2.1.}}</ref>

* The [[Picard group]] of line bundles on <math>\mathbb{P}(V)</math> is [[infinite cyclic]], and the [[tautological line bundle]] is a generator.

* In the case of projective space, where the tautological bundle is a [[line bundle]], the associated [[invertible sheaf]] of sections is <math>\mathcal{O}(-1)</math>, the tensor inverse (''ie'' the dual vector bundle) of the  hyperplane bundle or [[Proj#The twisting sheaf|Serre twist sheaf]] <math>\mathcal{O}(1)</math>; in other words the hyperplane bundle is the generator of the Picard group having positive degree (as a [[divisor (algebraic geometry)|divisor]]) and the tautological bundle is its opposite: the generator of negative degree.
